rv.q: This is a polished fantasy, extremely easy on the eye and a consummate midsummer comedy.
Godwin’s production is sweet, sparky, sexy, sombre and, in the end, touching in its depiction of the transformative power of love.
There are moments during Simon Godwin’s blissful revival of Much Ado, set in a fancy Sicilian hotel
Spending time at the Hotel Messina is a pleasure, a lazy holiday on which not a lot happens, very charmingly.
The glide of the action is delectable.
It’s a glittery, apolitical production but it’s well cast, stylish, summery stuff.
All part of the fun in church hall am-dram, perhaps — but not at the National Theatre.
For anyone who wants to see Parkinson, Heffernan or Godwin giving their best work, it’s sorely disappointing.
This whole production is a wonder too, and you will be just as helpless to resist.
You’ll wait years to see a better Benedick.
It’s all very larky and witty, with giggle-worthy sight gags involving a trolley, a hammock and a beach hut in the twin scenes that entrap Beatrice and Benedict into coupledom.
In the end, it’s a comedy that made the audience laugh out loud, and while this production isn’t perfect, it is nonetheless worth seeing.
This is light entertainment for a summer evening that takes us to Mediterranean sunshine while keeping us cool indoors.
If only the first half could match the clarity of the second the National’s production could be a hit.
However, Simon Godwin's new staging, transported from 16th century Sicily to an early 20th century Mediterranean Hotel, fails to fully ignite.
That’s the pleasure of a production like this: “leger” as the French group said, and gleefully farcical at times.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this visually stunning 1930s Sicilian hotel production. While most praise the gorgeous Art Deco design and period style, opinions split sharply on whether the leads have chemistry and if style overtakes substance.
